title: Mathiasella bupleuroides in bloom
description:
I like collecting and designing with unusual plants from cloud forests of Mexico/Central America, and this plant certainly fits the bill.  It has flowers that resemble Helleborus x argutifolius, but more graceful.  Named after the botanist Mildred Mathias of UCLA, it is a fairly recent discovery from Mexico, that has made its way into the horticulture trade here along the west coast USA.  It typically starts blooming in February or March, and can continue into June or July, and makes a large floppy stemmed evergreen herbaceous perennial that needs the support of surrounding shrubs or staking to look its best.  I like the way the Mathiasella is reaching out to "kiss" the vining tendrils of the Stauntonia hexaphylla vine against the blank wall of the courtyard.  The Stauntonia is related to the more familiar Akebia vine, and has the same tendencies of massive growth and beautiful foliage, while also having allegedly fragrant flowers(not noticeable to me), and edible fruit if you have more than one vine.  I used the Stauntonia here because I really like the character of the vine, and the way it adds a graceful sculptural presence against the wall, and the interesting two  toned foliage color.  Not a vine for the feint of heart, however, because it does require constant editing to keep it within bounds in a small space.

If you gotta have the Mathiasella plant, check out The Dry Garden Nursery on Shattuck Ave in Oakland, Richard Ward and Jimpa have a great stock of this plant that is hard to find anywhere else.

title: View upwards from a jacuzzi
description: I really enjoyed playing off the stark white walls of this home with expressive foliage of palms and other plantings.  In this case, the Trachycarpus fortunei, Chusan or Windmill Palm was planted in this spot to give a bit of privacy from a neighbor, as well to give a partial sense of overhead enclosure while in the jacuzzi.  I wanted to emphasize the design qualities of the foliage a bit, so I trimmed the leaf tips to give this perfectly symmetrical frond, while also removing browned leaf tips on the fronds from having been dug up, boxed and then replanted as a 36 inch box specimen in this garden.  I like the effect so much, I often do this with Trachycarpus even when the leaf tips are perfect!  Of course, it would be easier to just plant a Trachycarpus wagneriana, and save the labor to trim...
